subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statistical test is used for a test of difference, with an independent groups design and ordinal data?
questions.explain: The Mann-Whitney test is used for a difference with unrelated (independent) data at ordinal level.

questions.q: The sign test is used for a test of difference with:
options: Nominal data and a related (repeated measures) design
questions.explain: The sign test analyses a difference using nominal data from a related design, such as before-and-after categorical change.

questions.q: Which test is used for a test of difference, repeated measures design, with ordinal data?
questions.explain: The Wilcoxon signed-ranks test is used for a difference with related (repeated measures) data at ordinal level.

questions.q: For a sign test, the result is statistically significant when the calculated value is:
options: Always greater than the critical value
Equal to or less than the critical value at the relevant N and significance level
questions.explain: For the sign test the observed value must be equal to or less than the critical value (at the relevant N and p) to be significant.

questions.q: Systematic sampling involves:
options: Selecting whoever is most readily available
Selecting every nth person from a sampling frame
questions.explain: Systematic sampling selects every nth member (e.g. every 5th name) from an ordered list or sampling frame.

questions.q: Which of the following describes 'inter-observer reliability'?
options: The consistency of measurement across different observers
The extent to which an observation measures what it claims to
The number of behavioural categories used
questions.explain: Inter-observer reliability is the level of agreement between two or more observers recording the same behaviour.

questions.q: A correlational study differs from an experiment because it:
options: Measures the relationship between two co-variables without manipulating either
questions.explain: A correlation measures the strength and direction of a relationship between two co-variables but does not manipulate an IV, so causation cannot be inferred.

questions.q: In a laboratory experiment, the key defining feature compared with a field experiment is that:
options: Participants are unaware they are in a study
The study takes place in a controlled environment where extraneous variables can be tightly controlled
questions.explain: A lab experiment is conducted in a controlled setting allowing high control of extraneous variables, unlike a natural field setting.

questions.q: The standard deviation is a measure of:
options: Dispersion, showing the average spread of scores around the mean
questions.explain: Standard deviation is a measure of dispersion indicating how far, on average, scores deviate from the mean.

questions.q: Data measured on a scale with equal intervals but no true zero (e.g. temperature in Celsius) are at which level of measurement?
questions.explain: Interval data have equal intervals between points but no true zero, as in temperature measured in degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an extraneous variable and a confounding variable?
options: An extraneous variable is the same as the DV
Extraneous variables are always controlled; confounding variables never are
A confounding variable systematically varies with the IV and affects the DV, whereas an extraneous variable is any nuisance variable
questions.explain: A confounding variable varies systematically with the IV and so confuses results, while an extraneous variable is any other variable that could affect the DV.

questions.q: Which sampling method gives every member of the target population an equal chance of selection?
questions.explain: Random sampling, e.g. drawing names from a complete list, gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen.

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature that makes psychology 'scientific'?
options: Use of objectivity, replicability and empirical methods
questions.explain: Scientific psychology emphasises objectivity, empirical data, replicability and falsifiable hypotheses.

questions.q: A Type I error occurs when the researcher:
options: Rejects a true null hypothesis (a false positive)
Accepts a false null hypothesis (a false negative)
questions.explain: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true.

questions.q: Spearman's rho is the appropriate test when:
options: Testing a correlation with at least ordinal data
Testing a difference with a repeated measures design
Testing a difference with nominal data
questions.explain: Spearman's rho is a test of correlation used with at least ordinal-level data.

questions.q: A matched pairs design attempts to reduce which problem found in independent groups designs?
questions.explain: Matched pairs pairs participants on key variables before allocation, reducing the impact of participant variables.

questions.q: Which sampling method is most likely to produce a representative sample of a large population?
questions.explain: Stratified sampling reflects the proportions of subgroups in the population, increasing representativeness.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the null hypothesis?
options: To state that any difference or relationship is due to chance, i.e. no real effect
To predict the direction of the effect
questions.explain: The null hypothesis states there is no effect and that any observed difference is due to chance, and it is the hypothesis tested.

questions.q: A more stringent significance level (e.g. p ≤ 0.01) might be used when:
options: The research is exploratory and low-stakes
The consequences of a Type I error are particularly serious, such as in drug trials
questions.explain: A stricter level reduces the chance of a false positive and is used when wrongly accepting an effect would be costly.

questions.q: A Type II error occurs when the researcher:
options: Accepts (fails to reject) a false null hypothesis, a false negative
Sets the significance level too low
questions.explain: A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false.

questions.q: In psychology, the usual accepted level of statistical significance is:
questions.explain: The conventional significance level in psychology is p ≤ 0.05, meaning a 5% probability the result is due to chance.

questions.q: A pilot study is conducted in order to:
options: Replace the need for a control group
Test the final hypothesis with the full sample
Trial procedures and identify problems before the main study
questions.explain: A pilot study is a small-scale trial run to check and refine procedures, materials and design before the main study.

questions.q: A directional (one-tailed) hypothesis should be used when:
options: There is no previous research and findings are uncertain
Previous research suggests the direction of the difference or relationship
A null hypothesis cannot be written
questions.explain: A directional hypothesis is justified when prior research indicates which way the difference or correlation will go.

questions.q: In a questionnaire, a key advantage of closed questions over open questions is that they:
options: Produce quantitative data that is easy to analyse and compare
questions.explain: Closed questions yield quantitative data that are quick to analyse and compare, though they lack depth.

questions.q: A repeated measures design is one in which:
options: Participants are matched on relevant characteristics
Different participants are used in each condition
The same participants take part in all conditions
questions.explain: In a repeated measures design the same participants complete every condition of the experiment.

questions.q: To 'operationalise' a variable means to:
options: Control it as an extraneous variable
Define it precisely in terms of how it is measured or manipulated
questions.explain: Operationalisation means defining a variable clearly so it can be measured or manipulated, e.g. memory as 'number of words recalled'.

questions.q: Using a lenient significance level such as p ≤ 0.10 increases the risk of which error?
questions.explain: A more lenient level makes it easier to reject the null hypothesis, increasing the chance of a Type I error.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a covert observation?
options: Participants know they are being observed
Participants are unaware they are being observed
The observer takes part in the activity
Behaviour is recorded using closed questions
questions.explain: In a covert observation participants do not know they are being watched, which reduces demand characteristics but raises ethical concerns.

questions.q: 'Demand characteristics' refer to:
options: Features of the environment that distract participants
Cues that lead participants to guess the aim and change their behaviour
questions.explain: Demand characteristics are cues that help participants work out the study's purpose, potentially altering their behaviour.

questions.q: A particular weakness of a repeated measures design is:
options: It always requires a large sample
Order effects such as practice or fatigue
questions.explain: Because participants do all conditions, order effects (practice or fatigue) can confound the results, often countered by counterbalancing.
